Greed also walked straight into H, which ends with the large final cost of 9. The greedy algorithm has no way of knowing about costs that come later, so a late obstacle can make an early cheap-looking choice a bad one.

**A very small network makes the failure of greed easy to see.** From a start there are two routes to an end, each through one middle state. On the top route the first arrow costs 10 and the second costs 10. On the bottom route the first arrow costs only 2, but the second costs 100.
children: A greedy decision at the start compares 10 with 2 and picks the bottom route, then gets stuck paying 100. The totals are 20 for the top route and 102 for the bottom route, so the top route is five times cheaper even though its first step was five times more expensive.

Writing inside each middle state the cost of getting from that state to the end, 10 on top and 100 on the bottom, makes the decision at the start simple. Add the cost of the first arrow to the number stored in the state it leads to, and compare 20 with 102. Storing the cost of the rest of the journey inside each state removes the blindness of greed.

sections.title: Blank source page
Exhaustive search trades speed for certainty

teaching.text: **An exhaustive algorithm solves the shortest path problem by brute force.** It lists every possible route from start to end, adds up the cost of each one, and picks the smallest total. Nothing is skipped, so the answer is **guaranteed to be correct**.
children: The number of routes comes from multiplying the number of choices at each stage. From A there are 2 choices, from the second stage 3, from the third stage 3, and from the fourth stage only 1, so there are 18 complete routes. Each needs 3 additions to total, so checking every route takes 54 additions, followed by comparing 18 totals.

teaching.text: **The problem with exhaustive search is its growth.** Every added stage multiplies the number of routes by the number of choices at that stage, and every added state per stage makes each multiplier larger. With **many stages and many states** the number of routes explodes, and checking all of them takes a very, very long time.
children: Exhaustive search is accurate but impractical for large problems, while greedy search is fast but can be wrong. A method is needed that is both accurate and efficient.

sections.title: Bellman’s decomposition

teaching.text: **Bellman approached the problem by starting with an imaginary step.** Imagine we already knew the best possible cost of getting from B to J, and from C to J. These numbers are called VBJ and VCJ. The letter V stands for **Value**, and the Value of a state is the lowest total cost of getting from that state to the goal.

**If those two Values were known, the best cost from A to J, VAJ, would follow from one short calculation.** Any route out of A goes first to either B or C, since those are the only two arrows leaving A.
children: Going to B costs 12 for that arrow, and then the best possible rest of the trip is VBJ, so the best total through B is 12 plus VBJ. Going to C costs 7 and then VCJ, so the best total through C is 7 plus VCJ. The best cost from A is whichever of these two totals is smaller.

The word **min** means take the minimum, the smallest number in the set inside the braces. Each number in the set is built the same way, the cost of one arrow plus the Value of the state that arrow leads to.

sections.title: Solve the smaller problems that supply the values

teaching.text: **The difficulty is that we do not know VBJ or VCJ.** The rule for VAJ is correct, but it depends on two numbers that have not yet been found.

**Bellman's general strategy handles exactly this situation. To solve a problem, decompose it into subproblems you can solve.** Finding VAJ becomes two smaller problems, finding VBJ and finding VCJ. The phrase "if you can" matters. If a subproblem still cannot be solved directly, it gets broken down again into even smaller subproblems.

sections.title: Propagating known costs backward

teaching.text: **Bellman's reasoning at A applies in the same way at B.** We do not know the best cost from B to J, but if we knew the best costs from D, E and F to J, then we could find the best cost from B to J.
children: From B we can go to D for 5, to E for 6 or to F for 9. After each move, the best we can do is the Value of the state we arrived at. So VBJ is the minimum of 5 plus VDJ, 6 plus VEJ and 9 plus VFJ.
C works the same way with its arrows costing 14, 10 and 11, so VCJ is the minimum of 14 plus VDJ, 10 plus VEJ and 11 plus VFJ.

teaching.text: **These rules still depend on unknown Values, so the decomposition continues one more stage.** The Values of D, E and F depend on the Values of G, H and I.
children: VDJ is the minimum of 8 plus VGJ, 7 plus VHJ and 10 plus VIJ. VEJ is the minimum of 9 plus VGJ, 7 plus VHJ and 9 plus VIJ. VFJ is the minimum of 10 plus VGJ, 7 plus VHJ and 8 plus VIJ.

teaching.text: **At the fourth stage the subproblems finally become ones that can be solved directly.** Each of G, H and I has exactly one arrow, straight to J, so there is no decision to make and each Value is simply the cost of that arrow. VGJ is 5, VHJ is 9, and VIJ is 8.
children: The rules form a chain of dependence that runs from the end of the network back to the start. The known Values of G, H and I feed the rules for D, E and F. Those feed the rules for B and C, and those feed the single rule for A. Information about the cost of reaching J travels **backward** through the network, one stage at a time, starting from the states closest to the goal.

sections.title: Choose the best total after calculating values

teaching.text: **With the Values of G, H and I known, the Values of the third stage can be calculated directly.** For D the three totals are 8 plus 5, 7 plus 9 and 10 plus 8, so the minimum of 13, 16 and 18 gives VDJ of 13. For E the totals are 9 plus 5, 7 plus 9 and 9 plus 8, so VEJ is 14. For F the totals are 10 plus 5, 7 plus 9 and 8 plus 8, so VFJ is 15.
children: In all three cases the smallest total comes from going to G. G has the smallest Value of the fourth stage, 5, and that outweighs the differences in the arrow costs.

teaching.text: **The third-stage Values now go into the rules for B and C.** For B the totals are 5 plus 13, 6 plus 14 and 9 plus 15, so VBJ is 18. For C the totals are 14 plus 13, 10 plus 14 and 11 plus 15, so VCJ is 24. Finally, for A the totals are 12 plus 18 and 7 plus 24, which are 30 and 31, so VAJ is 30.
children: Every state now carries its Value. A is 30, B is 18, C is 24, D is 13, E is 14, F is 15, G is 5, H is 9, and I is 8.

teaching.text: **The best path comes from going greedy on the Values, not on the costs.** At each state, compare the options by adding the cost of the arrow to the Value of the state it leads to, and take the smallest sum. This is still a one-step-at-a-time choice, but now each option already includes the whole future.
children: At A, going to B gives 12 plus 18, which is 30, and going to C gives 7 plus 24, which is 31, so we go to **B** even though its arrow is the more expensive one. At B, going to D gives 18, to E gives 20, and to F gives 24, so we go to **D**. At D, going to G gives 13, to H gives 16, and to I gives 18, so we go to **G**. From G the only move is to J.
The best path is **A, B, D, G, J**, with total 12 plus 5 plus 8 plus 5, which equals 30 and matches VAJ exactly.

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming is this two-part method.** First, calculate the Values by working backward from the goal. Second, choose moves greedily using those Values. The method needed only one small minimum calculation per state instead of adding up all 18 routes one by one.

sections.title: A value summarizes the relevant future

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming is foresight about the whole route ahead.** Standing at the third stage, at D, E or F, greedy reasoning on arrow costs alone would often be pulled toward H, since the arrow into H costs 7 from every one of D, E and F, the cheapest or tied for cheapest. Dynamic programming reveals that **state H leads to something terrible**. The arrow out of H into J costs 9, the largest final cost in the network, so H has the largest Value in its stage.
children: At E, the arrow cost alone favors H at 7 over G at 9. Adding the Values changes the answer. Going to H gives 7 plus 9, which is 16, while going to G gives 9 plus 5, which is 14. The Value of H warns about the 9 before we ever reach it.

This warning still works if there are many more stages between the current state and J. However far away the bad cost lies, it has already been folded into the Values of every state that leads toward it.

teaching.text: **In the original problem, a late obstacle, the 9 on the arrow from H to J, caused an early greedy decision based on arrow cost to lead to a bad path.** The greedy algorithm picked C at the first step and ended up paying for that 9 at the last step.

**The Values contain the future.** Each Value already includes information about every obstacle between that state and the goal, so we can safely go greedy on them. The Values make **present decisions optimal**, since the whole future from each state is encapsulated in its Value.
children: **Søren Kierkegaard** wrote that life can only be understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards. Dynamic programming has exactly this structure. The Values are understood backwards, calculated from the goal toward the start. The decisions are lived forwards, made one at a time from A toward J.

sections.title: Recursive breakdown and reconstruction

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming starts by posing a problem, then its subproblems, then its sub-subproblems, and so on.** The big problem is solved by solving the subproblems, and the subproblems are solved by solving the sub-subproblems.
children: The big problem is finding VAJ. Its subproblems are finding VBJ and VCJ. Their subproblems are finding VDJ, VEJ and VFJ. Their subproblems are finding VGJ, VHJ and VIJ.

teaching.text: **The breakdown continues until the problems are trivial, meaning they can be answered with no calculation at all.** For G, H and I, the answer is simply the cost of the one arrow to J. Once the trivial problems are solved, we go back and solve the bigger problems, one level at a time, until we arrive at the original problem.

sections.title: The rule for propagating a value

teaching.text: **The bigger problems are solved by propagating Values from each stage to the stage before it using Bellman's idea.** To propagate means to pass information along, and here the information moves from later stages to the stages before them.

**Bellman's rule states that the Value at one state is the minimum of a set of numbers, each of which is the sum of the cost to one of the next states and the Value at that next state.** Every rule from VAJ down to VDJ, VEJ and VFJ follows this same pattern.
children: The rule starts with the stage just before the goal, where the Values are known directly. For each state in the stage before that, list every arrow leaving it, add each arrow's cost to the Value of the state where it ends, and keep the smallest sum as that state's Value. Repeat for the stage before, and stop when the starting state has its Value.

teaching.text: **Each state needs only a handful of additions and one comparison, and each Value is calculated once and reused by every state before it that connects to it.** VDJ of 13 is calculated once and then used in both the B rule and the C rule. This reuse is what keeps dynamic programming efficient when there are many stages and states.

sections.title: Least distance and least time can diverge

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming says to go through the bad 12 first to get onto a route that does not get stuck later at the 9.** Paying 12 to reach B instead of 7 to reach C looks like a mistake at the first step, but it puts us on the route with the lowest total. It may seem that making such a choice requires a big brain, since the decision-maker has to weigh the whole future against the present.

**The same trade-off appears when a lifeguard must reach a person.** When the lifeguard and the person are both on sand, the lifeguard runs at a **constant speed** the entire way, so the fastest route is the **shortest path**, a straight line. This holds whether the person is directly across the sand or off at an angle along the beach.
children: When the person is in the water, the speeds are **different**. The lifeguard runs fast on sand but swims slowly in water. The **path of least time** is no longer a straight line. The lifeguard runs a longer distance along the sand, reaching the water at a point closer to the swimmer, and then swims a short distance. The route bends at the water's edge.

The lifeguard's best route accepts a longer stretch of running, which looks worse by distance, to cut down the slow and costly swimming later. This is the same structure as paying 12 early to avoid the 9 at the end.

sections.title: Refraction shares the least-time principle

teaching.text: **Decision-making is like physics, and light makes the same choice.** Light behaves like the lifeguard in **refraction**, the bending of light as it passes from one material into another. Light travels **faster in air** and **slower in water**, and when it passes between them its path bends at the surface, just as the lifeguard's route bends at the water's edge.
children: This bending is why a pencil standing in a glass of water appears broken at the water line. The light coming from the underwater part of the pencil changes direction at the surface before reaching the eye.

teaching.text: **Light takes a path shaped the way the lifeguard's best route is shaped, with a bend at the boundary between a fast region and a slow region.** Light has no brain at all, so choosing a route that accepts an early cost to avoid a larger later one does not require a big brain. Physical systems arrive at these optimal paths on their own, and dynamic programming describes the same kind of optimal route through a series of stages.

sections.title: Reading the completed state values

teaching.text: **The complete solution can be written on the network by labeling each state with its Value and its best next state.** A is labeled 30 and B. B is labeled 18 and D, and C is labeled 24 and E. D is labeled 13 and G, E is labeled 14 and G, and F is labeled 15 and G. G, H and I are labeled 5 and J, 9 and J, and 8 and J.
**With these labels, the best route is read off by starting at A and following each state's best next state**, A to B, B to D, D to G, and G to J, for a total of 30.
children: The labels also give the best route from **any** state, not just from A. From C, the labels say to go to E, then G, then J, at a cost of 24. A single backward calculation solves the problem for every possible starting point at once.

sections.title: Pop quiz heading
Learning and coffee share approach to equilibrium

teaching.text: **A learning process can be tracked by plotting a quantity x against epochs, where an epoch is one round of learning in which x gets updated.** The **learning rate** controls how large each update is, and here it is 10 percent. Three runs start from different **initial conditions**, abbreviated **IC**.
children: The run with IC of 130 starts high and drops quickly toward about 80. The run with IC of 10 starts low and rises quickly toward about 80. The run with IC of 80 starts there and stays. Within roughly the first 25 to 50 epochs, all three runs meet, and from then until epoch 300 they fluctuate together in a narrow band around 80.

The final value does not depend on where the process starts. The initial condition only changes the early part of the curve. The changes are fastest at the beginning, when x is farthest from 80, and they slow down as x gets closer.

teaching.text: **Coffee changing temperature in a room follows the same pattern**, tracked as temperature against time over 8 minutes, with **room temperature at 18 degrees**.
children: Three cups of **hot coffee** start at 100, 80 and 60 degrees. All three cool toward room temperature, and by 8 minutes they are at roughly 29, 26 and 23 degrees. Three cups of **iced coffee** start at 10, 5 and 0 degrees. All three warm toward room temperature, and by 8 minutes they are all close to it, at roughly 16 to 17 degrees.

The hot coffee starting at 100 drops much faster at first than the one starting at 60. The larger the gap between the coffee and the room, the faster the temperature changes, and the change slows down as the gap shrinks.

teaching.text: **In both systems, many different starting values move toward the same final value**, about 80 for the learning process and 18 degrees for the coffee. The speed of change depends on how far the current value is from that final value.

sections.title: Dynamical Systems 3
Homework reminder
Position and velocity change each other

teaching.text: **A harmonic oscillator is built from only two quantities, x and v.** The quantity x is how far something is displaced from its resting point, and v is its **velocity**, how fast and in which direction x is moving. Neither variable is interesting alone. The whole system is about **how x and v change over time as a result of their relation to each other**.
**A dot over a variable means its change over time, in Isaac Newton's notation.** So ẋ is the change in x as time increases, and v̇ is the change in v as time increases.
children: The sign of the dotted quantity gives the direction of change. When ẋ is positive, x is rising, and when ẋ is negative, x is falling. The same holds for v.
The size of the dotted quantity gives how quickly the change happens. A large positive ẋ means x is climbing quickly, and a small positive ẋ means it is climbing slowly.

teaching.text: **The first rule says that the rate of change of x equals the current value of v, so ẋ is v.** Whatever sign v has at a given moment is the direction x moves at that moment. The quantity v directly steers x.

**The second rule says that the rate of change of v equals the negative of x, so v̇ is minus x.** The **minus sign** is the heart of the system. It means v is always pushed in the direction opposite to wherever x currently is.
children: The defining feature of the harmonic oscillator is that **x and v change each other**. The rate at which x changes is set by v, and the rate at which v changes is set by x. Neither variable can change on its own terms, and this two-way dependence is what produces repeating back-and-forth motion.

sections.title: Read the sign of the change

teaching.text: **Suppose that at some moment v equals negative 5.** The first rule gives ẋ equal to v, so ẋ is negative 5. The rate of change of x is negative, so x **will go down**. The value of x itself does not matter for this conclusion. Only the sign of v decides whether x is rising or falling.

**Now suppose that at some moment x equals negative 5.** The second rule gives v̇ equal to minus x, and minus negative 5 is positive 5. The two minus signs cancel, so the rate of change of v is positive, and v **will go up**.
children: This is the restoring behavior in action. When x is below zero, v is pushed upward, and an upward v then lifts x back toward zero through the first rule.
The example is why x and v must be read together. Knowing v tells what x is about to do, and knowing x tells what v is about to do.

teaching.text: **The same reading works for the positive cases.** When v is positive 5, ẋ is positive and x rises. When x is positive 5, v̇ is negative and v falls. These are statements about the direction of change, not about whether the current value is positive or negative. A velocity that is going up can be moving from a large negative value toward zero before it becomes positive.

sections.title: Two different sign relationships

teaching.text: **The two rules treat the sign differently.** The rule ẋ equals v keeps the sign. Positive velocity makes position rise, and negative velocity makes position fall. The rule v̇ equals minus x reverses the sign. Positive position makes velocity fall, and negative position makes velocity rise.

**Putting the two rules together, whenever x moves away from zero in either direction, the second rule turns v around, and the first rule then carries x back toward zero.** This **restoring relationship** is what keeps the system from drifting off and instead makes it swing back and forth.
children: The quantity changed by v̇ is velocity, not position. A positive position can go with a decreasing velocity even while the object is still moving toward larger positions. Keeping each quantity separate from its rate of change makes the back-and-forth motion understandable.

sections.title: Follow the position–velocity cycle

teaching.text: **The system can be followed moment by moment, starting with x at its highest positive value and v equal to zero.**
children: At the start, x is positive, so v̇ is negative and v begins to drop below zero. As soon as v is negative, ẋ is negative, so x starts to decrease, slowly at first since v is only slightly negative.
While x is still positive, v keeps getting more negative. A more negative v makes x fall faster, so x drops more and more steeply.
When x reaches zero, v̇ equals zero, so v stops decreasing. At this instant v is at its most negative value, which means x is crossing zero at its fastest speed.
Once x is below zero, v̇ becomes positive, so v starts rising back toward zero. The value x is still falling, but more and more slowly.
When v returns to zero, x has reached its lowest, most negative value. At that point x stops moving down and turns around.

With x negative, v keeps rising and becomes positive, so x climbs. The value v reaches its largest positive value just as x crosses zero on the way up, and then x returns to its maximum as v comes back to zero. The system is back where it started, and the whole cycle repeats.

teaching.text: **Computing the system at a series of separate moments gives a sequence of points, where each new value of x and v is worked out from the values just before it.** Connecting these points produces two smooth waves.
children: The x wave starts at the top, dips below zero to a lowest point, and climbs back up past zero to the top again. The v wave starts at zero, dips below zero to its lowest point, returns to zero, and then rises above zero.
The two waves have the same shape but are shifted in time by a quarter of a cycle. The value v is at its extremes exactly when x crosses zero, and v is zero exactly when x is at its extremes.

sections.title: A closed feedback loop

teaching.text: **A dynamical system is a set of variables together with rules for how those variables change over time.** The x-v system is a specific kind called an **oscillation** or **vibration dynamical system**. Oscillation and vibration mean the same thing here, a quantity repeatedly swinging back and forth around a middle value.

**The relationship can be drawn as a loop of influence, with x and v each in a circle.** One arrow runs from v to x, standing for ẋ equals v, since v determines how x changes. A second arrow runs from x back to v, standing for v̇ equals minus x, since x determines how v changes. The loop is closed, so a change in v changes x, and that change in x goes on to change v again.
children: The loop between x and v is enough, by itself, to generate the repeated swinging. Once the system is set in motion it keeps cycling without anything outside it having to push it again.

Plotted against time, x traces a wave that starts at its peak, falls below zero, rises back to the same peak, and repeats. Each cycle reaches the same height and the same depth, and each cycle takes the same amount of time. The value v follows the same kind of repeating wave over the same stretch of time.

sections.title: Homework reminder
Harmonic oscillators across systems

teaching.text: **The same two-variable structure of ẋ equals v and v̇ equals minus x shows up in a huge range of systems**, including the air in the vocal tract, the vocal folds, economies, music, and matter itself.

**Calling a system a harmonic oscillator means identifying something in it that plays the role of x, a displacement away from a resting state, and something that plays the role of v, the rate at which that displacement changes.** It also means accepting a simplification, since real systems are usually messier than two perfectly linked variables. The harmonic oscillator is still useful as a model, since it captures the basic back-and-forth pattern that all of these systems share.

sections.title: Compression and rarefaction of air

teaching.text: **The vocal tract is the air-filled passage from the vocal folds in the throat up through the mouth to the lips.** A thin slice of air inside it contains a large number of air particles, and **pressure** in this slice depends on how close together the particles are.
children: **High pressure** means the air particles are very close together. **Low pressure** means the air particles are very far apart. The particles themselves stay the same, in number and in size. The only thing that changes is the distance between them.

teaching.text: **Compression is the state in which particles are squeezed closer together than their normal spacing, and rarefaction is the state in which they are spread farther apart.** The normal spacing, where the air is neither squeezed nor stretched, is the **equilibrium spacing**.
children: Tracking one pair of neighboring particles, at equilibrium they sit at 100 percent of their equilibrium distance. At the strongest compression the pair is squeezed to about 56 percent of that distance, a little more than half as far apart as usual. At the strongest rarefaction the same pair is stretched to about 141 percent.

The slice cycles through these states continuously. It compresses, passes back through equilibrium, rarefies, and passes back through equilibrium again. In real speech the motion is much smaller than these exaggerated values, and the slice is an idealized piece of the air.

teaching.text: **The slice of air behaves like a harmonic oscillator.** The spacing of the particles, measured relative to equilibrium, plays the role of x. Air that is squeezed together tends to push itself apart, and air that is spread out tends to be pulled back together, so any departure from equilibrium spacing is pushed back toward equilibrium. This is the same restoring relationship as v̇ equals minus x, and it is why the slice keeps swinging between compression and rarefaction.

sections.title: Connect air motion to a cosine

teaching.text: **The back-and-forth motion of the air slice follows a cosine, so x equals the cosine of the phase.** Here x measures the **normalized expansion** of the slice. Normalized means the values are scaled so that the largest stretch equals plus 1 and the largest squeeze equals minus 1.
children: An x of plus 1 means the particles are **farthest apart**, maximum rarefaction. An x of 0 means the particles are at **equilibrium** spacing. An x of minus 1 means the particles are **closest together**, maximum compression. Any positive x means some degree of rarefaction, and any negative x means some degree of compression.

teaching.text: **The phase is the position within a cycle, and one complete cycle corresponds to the phase increasing by 2π.** Running the phase from 0 to 6π covers exactly three full cycles, ending at 2π, 4π and 6π.
children: At phase 0 the cosine equals plus 1, so the slice is at maximum rarefaction. As the phase increases, x decreases. A value such as plus 0.74 means the particles are still farther apart than equilibrium, but less so than at the start.

At phase π over 2 the cosine equals 0, so the slice passes through equilibrium. A value such as minus 0.54 means the slice is now compressed. At phase π the cosine equals minus 1, so the slice reaches maximum compression.

At phase 3π over 2, x returns to 0, and at phase 2π, x is back at plus 1, completing the pattern of maximum rarefaction, then compression, then rarefaction again. Over the next two cycles x passes through values such as plus 0.31, minus 0.05, minus 0.21 and plus 0.45, and each value's sign says whether the slice is rarefied or compressed at that moment.

teaching.text: **The cosine is the same wave that the x-v system produces when x starts at its maximum and v starts at zero.** In both cases the curve begins at the top and swings downward. So the vibrating air in the vocal tract follows the harmonic oscillator relationship, and its expansion over time traces a cosine.

sections.title: Vowels depend on tongue position

teaching.text: **Vowels differ from one another in where the tongue sits inside the vocal tract.** These positions can be imaged with magnetic resonance imaging, which produces a side view of the head cut down the middle, with the speaker facing left, the tongue as the large bright mass in the mouth, and the dark regions as air.

**Vowels are organized along two dimensions, height and frontness.** **Height** is whether the tongue body is raised toward the roof of the mouth, **high**, or lowered, **low**. **Frontness** is whether the tongue body is pushed forward toward the teeth, **front**, pulled back toward the throat, **back**, or held in between, **central**.
children: In **"dean,"** the vowel is **high and front**. The tongue body is raised and pushed forward, close to the hard roof of the mouth, which leaves a large open air space in the throat behind the tongue.
In **"dune,"** the vowel is **high and back**. The tongue is still raised, but its highest point is pulled back toward the soft rear part of the roof of the mouth.

In **"Dan,"** the vowel is **low and front**. The tongue is lowered and the mouth is more open, with the tongue body still toward the front. In **"Don,"** the vowel is **low and back**. The tongue is lowered and pulled back into the throat, which narrows the air space behind it.
In **"done,"** the vowel is **central**. The tongue rests in the middle of the mouth, neither strongly raised nor lowered and neither pushed forward nor pulled back.

teaching.text: **Each tongue position gives the air in the vocal tract a different shape.** A differently shaped column of air vibrates in a different way, and that difference in vibration is what makes one vowel sound different from another.

sections.title: Vowels combine more than one vibration

teaching.text: **A single cosine describes air vibrating at one frequency, but a vowel is more complex.** The air in the vocal tract vibrates at **several frequencies at the same time**, and the vowel is the **sum** of those vibrations. Since each vibration is a cosine, and each cosine is the behavior of a harmonic oscillator, a vowel can be modeled as **harmonic oscillators added together**.
children: **Frequency** is the number of complete cycles a vibration makes per second, measured in **hertz (Hz)**. A vibration at f hertz is written as the cosine of 2π times f times t, where t is time in seconds. Multiplying by 2π converts the number of cycles into phase, since one full cycle equals a phase of 2π.

teaching.text: **The vowel /i/, the vowel in "dean," is modeled as a 1 Hz vibration plus a 4 Hz vibration, the cosine of 2πt plus the cosine of 8πt.** The first term is the 1 Hz vibration, since 2π times 1 is 2π, and the second is the 4 Hz vibration, since 2π times 4 is 8π. The result is a slow wave with fast ripples riding on top of it. Over 3 seconds, the slow component completes 3 cycles while the fast component completes 12.

**The vowel /a/, the vowel in "Don," is modeled as a 2 Hz vibration plus a 3 Hz vibration, the cosine of 4πt plus the cosine of 6πt.** Over 3 seconds the 2 Hz component completes 6 cycles and the 3 Hz component completes 9. The two frequencies are close together, so the sum produces a different repeating pattern of tall and short swings than /i/ does.

**These frequencies are example values, not measured vowel frequencies.** They are chosen low enough that the motion can be watched, and the two components in each vowel have **equal amplitudes**, each swinging between plus 1 and minus 1.
children: Since each component reaches at most plus 1 and at least minus 1, their sum ranges between plus 2 and minus 2. The sum reaches plus 2 only when both cosines peak at the same moment, which for both vowels happens at 0, 1, 2 and 3 seconds, since every component completes a whole number of cycles in each second.

At other moments the components partly cancel or partly reinforce each other. At one moment /i/ can be at minus 1.21 while /a/ is at plus 0.58, and at another /i/ can be at plus 0.62 while /a/ is at minus 1.62.

teaching.text: **The same sign rule from the single cosine still applies.** **Positive x means rarefaction**, with particles farther apart than equilibrium, and **negative x means compression**, with particles closer together. For /i/ and /a/, the slice of air is squeezed and stretched in two different time patterns, and those two patterns are what distinguish the two vowels. Watching them at one-quarter speed makes the different rhythms visible.

sections.title: Praat demonstration

teaching.text: **Praat is a free computer program used in phonetics to record and analyze speech.** It displays the **waveform** of a recorded sound, the air pressure changing over time, and it can break that sound into the frequencies it contains.

**Recording vowels such as those in "dean" and "Don" in Praat shows the combined vibrations directly.** Each vowel produces its own repeating waveform, and each waveform is made of several frequencies added together, the same idea as the two-frequency models of /i/ and /a/.

sections.title: Two vibrating parts of speech

teaching.text: **During speech, two things vibrate.** The first is the air in the vocal tract, the vibration modeled by the cosines and sums of cosines. The second is the **vocal folds**.

**The vocal folds are two folds of tissue in the larynx, the voice box in the throat.** When air from the lungs pushes up against the closed folds, pressure builds until the folds are forced apart. Once they open and air rushes through, the pressure between them drops and the folds come back together. The cycle repeats many times per second.
children: This repeated opening and closing is itself an oscillation, with the folds swinging away from their closed position and being pulled back again.

Each opening lets a puff of air through, so the vocal folds chop the steady airflow from the lungs into a rapid series of puffs. Those puffs set the air in the vocal tract vibrating, and the shape of the vocal tract, set by the tongue position, determines which combination of frequencies that air vibrates at.

teaching.text: **Speech sounds such as vowels therefore come from one oscillator driving another.** The vocal folds vibrate, and the air in the vocal tract vibrates in response. The folds are moving tissue, while the air is undergoing changing compression and rarefaction, so an explanation of speech must account for both.

sections.title: Economic cycles around a growth trend

teaching.text: **The harmonic oscillator pattern also appears in the business cycle, the repeated rise and fall of economic activity over time.** The business cycle is plotted with **time** on the horizontal axis and the **level of real output** on the vertical axis. **Real output** is the total amount of goods and services an economy produces, adjusted so that price changes do not distort the comparison across years.
children: At a **peak**, output is at a high point. During a **recession**, output falls. At a **trough**, output reaches a low point. During a **recovery**, output rises again until the next peak. The sequence then repeats from the start.

teaching.text: **The swings happen around a rising straight line labeled trend or growth.** Over the long run output tends to increase, so each later peak can be higher than the one before. The oscillation is the part of output that swings above and below this trend line, so repeated fluctuation can coexist with an overall increase.
children: To treat the business cycle as a harmonic oscillator, the distance of output above or below the trend plays the role of x. Output above the trend is followed by a fall back toward and below it, and output below the trend is followed by a rise back toward and above it, the same back-and-forth pattern produced by ẋ equals v and v̇ equals minus x.

sections.title: Meadows reading reminder
Music and vibration

teaching.text: **Music is built from harmonic oscillators.** Every musical note is a vibration at a particular frequency. A plucked string, the column of air inside a wind instrument, and a vibrating reed each swing back and forth around a resting state, just as x does in the x-v system.
**The pitch of a note corresponds to its frequency.** A higher-pitched note vibrates more times per second, and a lower-pitched note vibrates fewer times per second.
children: Sheet music is a written record of which vibrations to produce and when. When several notes sound together, their vibrations add, the same way the 1 Hz and 4 Hz cosines add to form the model of /i/.

sections.title: Atoms, shell pictures and wave modes

teaching.text: **The harmonic oscillator appears in physics at the scale of atoms as the quantum harmonic oscillator.** In quantum physics a vibrating system cannot vibrate with just any amount of energy. It can only take certain specific energy levels, which is what **quantized** means.

**Matter is made up of atoms with different numbers of electrons, some vibrating at a low frequency and some at a high frequency.** In the quantum description, electrons in an atom are not tiny balls on tracks but **wave modes**, specific allowed patterns of vibration.

**Magnesium shows two ways of drawing an atom.** A neutral magnesium atom has 12 **electrons**, and its nucleus contains 12 **protons**. Its **ground-state configuration**, the arrangement of electrons at lowest energy, is written 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s².
children: In the older **solar system** drawing, also called the **Bohr-style shell** drawing, electrons are particles that travel on circular paths around the nucleus, arranged in shells of 2, 8 and 2. This is a historical model of how the shells are arranged.

In the **quantum orbital** description, each occupied wave mode, called an **orbital**, contributes a cloud of **electron density** around the nucleus. Darker shading is greater density, a region where an electron is more likely to be found.

The **total electron density** of magnesium is built by adding together the densities of all its occupied orbitals, 1s², 2s², 2p⁶ and 3s². The superscript counts the electrons in each orbital group, and 2p⁶ includes all three filled p orbitals. The sum is a sum of **probability densities**, and the sizes and shading contrasts are drawn schematically rather than to exact scale. The innermost 1s electrons form the densest cloud close to the nucleus, the 2s and 2p electrons form a middle layer, and the 3s electrons form the faint outermost layer.

teaching.text: **Atomic orbitals are quantized wave modes, which connects them to the idea of vibration, but magnesium is not a harmonic-oscillator atom.** The quantum harmonic oscillator is a specific model, and real atoms like magnesium follow related but different rules.

sections.title: Python position–velocity demonstration

teaching.text: **The x-v system can be computed step by step in Python, producing the same sequence of points traced through time.** The system starts with x at its maximum and v at zero, and time is divided into many small steps of size dt.
children: At each step, ẋ is set equal to the current v, following the first rule, and v̇ is set equal to the negative of the current x, following the second rule.
The new x is the old x plus ẋ multiplied by the step size, and the new v is the old v plus v̇ multiplied by the step size.
Repeating this many times builds up the full x wave and v wave one small step at a time. Smaller steps make the computed points follow the true smooth waves more closely.

teaching.text: **The program uses numpy for the arrays and matplotlib for the plot.** It sets dt to 0.01 and the number of steps to 1000, fills two arrays with zeros, sets x[0] to 1.0 and v[0] to 0.0, and then loops over the steps. Inside the loop, x_dot takes the value of v[n], v_dot takes the value of minus x[n], and the next entries are x[n] plus x_dot times dt and v[n] plus v_dot times dt. Finally it plots x and v against t.

**The plotted output reproduces the behavior of the harmonic oscillator.** The value x starts at the top and traces a cosine wave, and v starts at zero, drops negative first, and traces the same wave shape shifted by a quarter of a cycle. The value v reaches its extremes whenever x crosses zero, and v passes through zero whenever x reaches its extremes.

sections.title: Dynamical Systems 5
Two quantities in an oscillator

teaching.text: **A harmonic oscillator is a dynamical system with two variables that feed into each other, position, written x, and velocity, written v.** Position tells where something is, and velocity tells how fast and in which direction it is moving. The system is fully described by two rules of change, one for each variable, and each rule depends on the other variable.
children: The dot above a letter is the notation for change over time. So ẋ is the **increase or decrease in x with time**, the rate at which position is changing at a given moment, and v̇ is the rate at which velocity is changing.

teaching.text: **The first rule says that the rate of change of position equals the velocity, so ẋ is v.** In other words, velocity drives position. When v is positive, x grows, and when v is negative, x shrinks. When v is exactly zero, x holds still for that instant. In the loop diagram this is the red arrow from v to x, which marks v as the cause and x as the thing being changed.

**The second rule says that the rate of change of velocity equals the negative of the position, so v̇ is minus x.** Position drives velocity, but with a minus sign. When x is positive, velocity is pushed downward, and when x is negative, velocity is pushed upward. This is the blue arrow from x to v. Together the red and blue arrows form a **closed loop of mutual influence**. The value v changes x, and x changes v, over and over.
**Stepping through the loop by hand from x at 1 and v at 0 works out what it does.** At the very start, position is at its highest value and nothing is moving yet.
children: Since x is 1, the second rule gives v̇ of negative 1, so velocity starts decreasing and becomes negative. Once v is negative, the first rule says ẋ is negative, so position begins to fall, slowly at first and then faster and faster as v grows more negative.

Position keeps falling until it crosses zero. At the moment x is 0, the second rule gives v̇ of 0, so velocity stops changing. This is the moment when velocity is at its most negative, which means position is falling at its fastest right as it passes through zero.

After the crossing, x is negative, so v̇ is now positive. Velocity starts climbing back toward zero, which means position is still falling but more slowly. When velocity reaches zero, position stops falling at its lowest point, negative 1. From there velocity turns positive, position starts to rise, and the whole sequence runs in reverse until x is back at plus 1 with v at 0.

teaching.text: **Plotting both variables against time point by point gives two waves.** Position starts at its peak of plus 1, drops through zero, bottoms out at negative 1, and comes back up to its peak. Velocity starts at zero, dips negative, returns to zero, rises positive, and comes back to zero.
children: The two waves are offset by a quarter of a cycle. **Velocity is zero whenever position is at a peak or a trough**, and **velocity is at its largest size whenever position is crossing zero**. This offset is a direct consequence of the two rules. Position turns around only when velocity reaches zero, and velocity turns around only when position reaches zero.

sections.title: Repeated change in a loop

teaching.text: **An oscillation, also called a vibration, is a repeating back-and-forth motion around a central point.** The two-variable loop between x and v is the basic dynamical system that produces it. Each variable pushes on the other, and the result is that neither one ever settles down.
children: When the loop is drawn with one arrow from x to v and another from v back to x, the influence is **circular**. There is no single cause at the start and no single effect at the end.

Graphed smoothly over time, x traces a wave that starts high, swings down below zero, swings back up, and continues through repeated cycles. The value v traces a wave of the same shape that starts at zero and heads negative first, staying a quarter cycle out of step with x.

teaching.text: **The key property of this system is that it never comes to rest on its own.** In the systems from the first dynamical-systems material, variables moved toward a resting value and stopped there. Here, every time one variable reaches its target, the other variable is at its largest value and pushes it past the target again.
children: Position overshoots zero because velocity is at its maximum at the moment position reaches zero. Velocity overshoots zero because position is at its maximum at the moment velocity reaches zero. That is why the motion keeps repeating.

sections.title: Why a spring and a mass make vibration

teaching.text: **Physically, vibration requires two effects working together.** Neither one alone can produce a back-and-forth motion.

**The first effect is a spring, more precisely a viscous spring.** A spring is the springiness found in many objects, their tendency to return to a natural shape or position after being pushed or pulled. The word "viscous" refers to a frictional, slowing quality, and it is set aside here to focus on the springiness itself.
children: A spring has a property called **stiffness**. Stiffness measures how strongly the spring pulls back toward its natural position when it has been moved away from it. A very stiff spring pulls back hard, and a loose spring pulls back gently.

teaching.text: **The second effect is mass.** Mass is the amount of matter in an object, and it determines how the object carries motion once it is moving.
**Vibration matters because it shows up across many different systems, both physical and abstract.**
children: **The jolt we feel when a car hits a bump** is a vibration, produced by the car's suspension springs and the car's mass together. **Music** is vibration, since strings, air columns and drum skins all vibrate to produce sound. **Boom and bust in economics** is a vibration, with an economy swinging above and below a steady level in repeating cycles.

**Oscillation in SGD** is a vibration. SGD stands for **stochastic gradient descent**, a method used to train machine-learning models by repeatedly nudging a value toward a target. Under some settings, that value swings back and forth around the target rather than settling onto it.
**The motion of the air in the vocal tract and the motion of the vocal folds during speech** are vibrations. Every sound produced in talking is built from these vibrations.

sections.title: Air particles move closer and farther apart

teaching.text: **The air inside the vocal tract can be treated as a small slice of material made of many particles.** During speech, the particles in the slice stay the same, and each particle stays the same size. **What changes is the distance between the particles.**
children: At **equilibrium spacing**, the particles sit at their natural, resting distance from one another. A chosen pair of neighboring particles is at 100 percent **of its equilibrium distance**. The equilibrium size of the slice is the reference that all other states are compared with.

teaching.text: **Compression is the state in which the particles are pushed closer together than their resting distance.** In a compressed slice, the chosen pair sits at only 56 percent of its equilibrium distance, and the whole slice shrinks. **High pressure means air that is packed very close together**, so compression is a high-pressure state.

**Rarefaction is the state in which the particles are spread farther apart than their resting distance.** In a rarefied slice, the chosen pair sits at 144 percent of its equilibrium distance, and the whole slice expands. **Low pressure means air that is spread very far apart**, so rarefaction is a low-pressure state.

**During speech, a slice of air in the vocal tract alternates between compression and rarefaction, shrinking and expanding around its equilibrium size again and again.** This alternation is a vibration of the air. The sizes in this model are idealized and exaggerated so that the change in spacing is visible. Real air in the vocal tract changes its spacing by much smaller amounts.

sections.title: Balancing feedback reduces displacement

teaching.text: **The spring effect on its own can be written as a single rule of change, ẋ equals minus one third of x.** Here x is the distance of the spring from its natural position, and ẋ is how fast that distance is changing. The rate of change is always **one third of the current distance, with the opposite sign**.
children: **If x is positive, ẋ is negative, so x falls.** A spring stretched in the positive direction moves back toward zero. **If x is negative, ẋ is positive, so x rises.** A spring compressed in the negative direction also moves back toward zero, just from the other side.

teaching.text: **The rule can be followed step by step from an initial condition of x equal to 1.** The initial condition is the value the system starts from before any change has happened.
children: With x at 1, x will **fall by one third of its current size**. One third of 1 is one third, so x drops to two thirds. One third of two thirds is two ninths, so x drops to four ninths. One third of four ninths is four twenty-sevenths, so x drops to eight twenty-sevenths.
The process repeats **again and again**, and each drop is smaller than the one before it. The first drop was one third, the second was two ninths, and the third was four twenty-sevenths.

teaching.text: **When x is smaller, ẋ, its speed of falling, is smaller too.** The spring moves quickly when it is far from its natural position and slows down as it gets closer.
children: Graphed against time, x starts at 1 and curves downward toward zero. The slope is steeply negative at the start and becomes **smaller and smaller negative** as time goes on. The curve gets closer and closer to zero but **never crosses it**, since the speed shrinks to nothing as the distance shrinks to nothing.

If the initial condition is negative, the same logic runs the other way. Starting below zero, x rises toward zero, quickly at first and then more slowly, with a slope that is **smaller and smaller positive**, and again never crosses it.

teaching.text: **This kind of system has a natural resting condition, which here is x at 0.** When the system's position is at a **discrepancy** with its natural position, meaning it has been moved away from where it rests, it **feeds back on itself** through the rule to cancel that discrepancy. This is **negative feedback**, also called **balancing feedback**, from Meadows' work on systems.
children: The feedback is called negative because the change always opposes the discrepancy. A positive discrepancy produces a negative change, and a negative discrepancy produces a positive change. It is called balancing because its effect is to bring the system back into balance at its resting point.

**These are systems that are in motion only in order to achieve their equilibrium.** An **equilibrium** is a state where the system has no reason to change any further. A spring moves only because it is away from its natural position, and once it arrives there, all motion stops.

teaching.text: **The number minus one third in the rule is the stiffness, and its size controls how quickly the spring returns to equilibrium.** A **higher stiffness**, a larger fraction than one third, means the spring closes a bigger share of the remaining distance at every step, so it returns to zero faster. A **lower stiffness** means it closes a smaller share at every step, so it returns more slowly.

sections.title: Mass carries motion onward

teaching.text: **Mass behaves very differently from a spring. If a mass is moving, it just keeps on moving.** A mass does not need a discrepancy or a target to keep going, and it has no natural resting position that it is trying to reach.

**This principle was worked out by Galileo, Descartes and Newton. A mass in motion stays in motion.** Without an outside force acting on it, a moving object continues at the same speed in the same direction.
children: Motion of this kind is called **constant velocity**. An object with constant velocity covers **the same distance in every equal interval of time**. A car rolling along a straight street at constant velocity passes the same amount of scenery in every moment. It does not speed up, slow down or stop on its own.

teaching.text: **This property is exactly what the spring lacks.** A spring slows down as it nears its resting point and stops there, while a mass carries its motion forward regardless of where it is.

sections.title: Returning to a place versus passing through it

teaching.text: **A spring stops at a place, while a mass stops after a process.** The spring's stopping point is a location, its natural position. A mass does not stop at a location at all. It keeps moving until something removes its motion over time.

**Consider a spring attached to a wall at one end, lying on a table, with no mass on its free end.** Its displacement x is **measured from the spring's natural position**, set as x equal to 0, and the scale runs from negative 1 to plus 1.
children: When the free end is pulled out to plus 1 and released, the spring **returns and stops at zero**. The end approaches zero **without crossing it**. Graphed over time, this return is a curve that starts at plus 1 and bends down toward zero, flattening as it gets close, the same shape as the curve produced by the one-third rule.

When the free end is instead pushed to negative 1 and released, **x rises toward zero without crossing it**. Pulling the spring out again gives the exact same return each time. A spring alone always settles at its natural position and never overshoots.

teaching.text: **When a mass is attached to the free end of the same spring and the system is released from plus 1, the result is completely different.** The spring still pulls the mass back toward zero, but when the mass reaches zero it is moving at its fastest, and **the mass carries that motion through the crossing**.
children: The mass continues past zero into negative displacement. Now the spring is stretched the other way, so it pulls back toward zero from the negative side. The mass slows down, stops near negative 1, and is pulled back through zero toward the positive side again. This repeats through **every crossing**.

teaching.text: **Graphed over time, the spring-plus-mass system produces a lightly damped oscillation.** The curve swings from plus 1 down below zero, back up above zero, and continues through repeated cycles.
children: **Damping** is the gradual loss of motion over time, which comes from the viscous, frictional part of the spring. In a lightly damped system the damping is small, so each swing is only a little smaller than the one before and the oscillation continues for many cycles. Eventually the damping would bring the mass to rest at zero, which is what it means for a mass to stop after a process.

teaching.text: **Putting the two effects together recovers the harmonic oscillator.** The spring supplies the pull back toward the natural position, the rule v̇ equals minus x, since the farther the mass is from zero, the harder its velocity is pushed back. The mass supplies persistent motion, the rule ẋ equals v, since position keeps changing as long as there is velocity, including at the moment the mass passes through zero.
children: A spring alone gives balancing feedback that ends at equilibrium. A mass alone gives motion that never turns around. **A spring and a mass together give vibration**, since the spring keeps turning the motion around and the mass keeps carrying it past the resting point.

sections.title: Air expansion follows a cosine

teaching.text: **The vibration of a slice of air in the vocal tract can be described with a single mathematical function, the cosine.** The value x measures the **normalized expansion** of the slice, how far the particles are spread relative to their equilibrium spacing, scaled so that the extremes are plus 1 and minus 1. So x equals the cosine of the phase.
children: An x of plus 1 means the particles are **farthest apart**, **maximum rarefaction**. An x of 0 means the particles are at their **equilibrium** spacing. An x of minus 1 means the particles are **closest together**, **maximum compression**.

teaching.text: **The phase is the input to the cosine, and it tracks where the slice is within its cycle of motion.** One full cycle of the cosine takes a phase of 2π, so a phase running from 0 to 6π covers exactly **three cycles**.
children: At a phase of 0 the cosine equals plus 1, so the slice starts at maximum rarefaction. At a phase of π the cosine equals minus 1, so the slice has reached maximum compression halfway through the first cycle. At a phase of 2π the cosine is back at plus 1, completing Cycle 1. The same pattern repeats for Cycle 2, ending at 4π, and Cycle 3, ending at 6π.

The slice therefore moves from **maximum rarefaction to compression and back to rarefaction** in every cycle, following the cosine curve exactly. Partway through a swing it is in an in-between state. At plus 0.84 the particles are still rarefied but not at their maximum spread, and at minus 0.84 they are compressed but not at their tightest.

teaching.text: **This cosine is the same wave that position traced in the harmonic oscillator**, starting at its peak and swinging down through zero to its lowest point and back. The air in the vocal tract behaves as a harmonic oscillator, with the springiness of the air pushing it back toward equilibrium spacing and the mass of the air carrying it past equilibrium each time.
children: The sizes of the slice in this model are exaggerated and its motion is slowed, so that each stage of the cycle is visible. The dashed boundary marks the slice's equilibrium size.

sections.title: Compare tongue configurations for vowels

teaching.text: **Different vowels are made by placing the tongue in different positions inside the vocal tract.** Side-view MRI images of the head during five words show how the tongue body moves to create each vowel. The vowels are organized along two dimensions, **height**, how high or low the tongue body sits in the mouth, and **front or back**, how far forward or backward it sits.

**High vowels are made with the tongue body raised close to the roof of the mouth.** In **"dean,"** the vowel is **high and front**. The tongue body is pushed up and forward toward the hard palate, leaving a wide open space in the throat behind the tongue. In **"dune,"** the vowel is **high and back**. The tongue body is raised but bunched toward the back of the mouth, closer to the soft palate.

**Low vowels are made with the tongue body lowered away from the roof of the mouth.** In **"Dan,"** the vowel is **low and front**. The tongue sits lower while staying toward the front, leaving a large open space above it. In **"Don,"** the vowel is **low and back**. The tongue is lowered and pulled back toward the throat, which narrows the space behind the tongue.
children: In **"done,"** the vowel is **central**. The tongue body sits in a middle position, neither pushed far forward nor pulled far back.

teaching.text: **Each tongue position gives the air inside the vocal tract a different shape.** A different shape changes how the air vibrates, and those differences in vibration are what make one vowel sound different from another.

sections.title: Frequency counts cycles in a fixed interval

teaching.text: **The frequency of a vibration is how many complete cycles it goes through in a given amount of time.** Three vibrations can be compared over the same 12-second interval, each covering the same range of particle spacing and each starting at **maximum rarefaction**, where x is plus 1. As before, plus 1 is maximum rarefaction, 0 is equilibrium, and minus 1 is maximum compression.

**The low-frequency vibration completes 3 cycles in 12 seconds.** Each cycle takes 4 seconds, so its peaks fall at 0, 4, 8 and 12 seconds, and its frequency is 3 cycles in 12 seconds, or 0.25 cycles per second.

**The mid-frequency vibration completes 6 cycles in 12 seconds.** Each cycle takes 2 seconds, so the slice swings between rarefaction and compression twice as often as the low-frequency one, at 0.5 cycles per second.

**The high-frequency vibration completes 9 cycles in 12 seconds.** Each cycle takes 12 ninths of a second, about 1.33 seconds, so this slice swings the most rapidly of the three, at 0.75 cycles per second.

**All three vibrations reach the same extremes of rarefaction and compression. The only thing that differs among them is how quickly the cycle repeats.** Frequency is a separate property from how far the particles spread or squeeze, and a vibration can be made faster or slower without changing its range.
children: One cycle per second is called **one hertz**, written **Hz**. This unit is used for the frequencies in the vowel models.

sections.title: Different combinations give different vowel patterns

teaching.text: **A vowel is not a single cosine. A vowel can be modeled as a sum of vibrations at different frequencies happening at the same time in the same slice of air.** The simplest model uses two frequencies of equal size added together, and the two frequencies chosen give each vowel its own pattern of motion.
children: The frequencies in these models are small example values, chosen so the combined wave is easy to follow. They are not the actual frequencies found in speech.

A cosine at a frequency of f hertz is written as the cosine of 2π times f times t, where t is time in seconds. Since one cycle takes a phase of 2π, multiplying 2π by f gives f full cycles for every second that passes. A 1 Hz vibration is the cosine of 2πt, which completes one cycle at 1 second. A 4 Hz vibration is the cosine of 8πt, which completes four cycles at 1 second.

teaching.text: **The vowel /i/, the vowel in "dean," is modeled as a 1 Hz vibration plus a 4 Hz vibration, the cosine of 2πt plus the cosine of 8πt.** At time 0 both cosines equal plus 1, so the sum is 2. The combined wave starts at plus 2, **maximum rarefaction** for the combined motion, and the range of x is now from plus 2 to minus 2, since two waves of size 1 are stacked together.
children: At 0.5 seconds, the 1 Hz wave is halfway through its cycle and the 4 Hz wave has completed exactly two cycles, so the sum is the cosine of π plus the cosine of 4π, which is minus 1 plus 1, or 0.

Between its large peaks, the /i/ wave has a busy pattern. It rises to smaller peaks near plus 1, dips to troughs near minus 1.7, and touches zero at the halfway point. The fast 4 Hz wave rides on top of the slow 1 Hz wave, putting several smaller wiggles inside each slow cycle. The whole pattern repeats **once every second**, returning to plus 2 at 1, 2 and 3 seconds.

teaching.text: **The vowel /a/, close to the vowel in "Don," is modeled as a 2 Hz vibration plus a 3 Hz vibration, the cosine of 4πt plus the cosine of 6πt.** At time 0 both cosines equal plus 1, so /a/ also starts at plus 2, maximum rarefaction.
children: At 0.5 seconds, the 2 Hz wave has completed exactly one cycle and the 3 Hz wave one and a half cycles, so the sum is the cosine of 2π plus the cosine of 3π, which is 1 plus negative 1, or 0.

The /a/ wave has a different shape from /i/. Between each large peak at plus 2, it drops to a deep trough near minus 1.6, rises to a pair of small humps near plus 0.7 separated by a dip to zero, drops to another deep trough, and returns to plus 2. This pattern also repeats **once every second**.

teaching.text: **In both vowels, positive x means rarefaction and negative x means compression.** Both vowels start at the same value and repeat at the same rate, yet the air moves in a clearly different way within each second. **The combination of frequencies is what distinguishes one vowel from another.** The motion in these models is played back at one quarter of its speed so that the particle spacing can be followed.

sections.title: Predict the effect of mass and stiffness

teaching.text: **Perturbation theory is the study of how a system's behavior changes when one of its parameters is nudged up or down.** A **parameter** is a fixed setting of a system, such as how heavy the mass is or how stiff the spring is. For a mass-spring system, the behavior of interest is its **frequency**, how many oscillations it completes per second.

**If the mass m of a mass-spring system is increased, the frequency decreases.** A heavier mass carries its motion more strongly, so the spring takes longer to slow it down and turn it around at each end of its swing. Each cycle takes longer, and fewer cycles fit into each second. **More mass means a lower frequency.**

**If the stiffness k of the spring is increased, the frequency increases.** A stiffer spring pulls back harder on the mass for the same displacement, so it turns the mass around more quickly at each end of its swing. Each cycle takes less time, and more cycles fit into each second. **More stiffness means a higher frequency.**

**These two results are the core perturbation-theory relationships for a mass-spring system.** Increasing mass lowers frequency, and increasing stiffness raises frequency. They give a way to predict how a vibrating system will sound or behave just from knowing whether it is heavy or light and stiff or loose.

sections.title: Hearing separates a mixture into frequencies

teaching.text: **The mass-spring relationships explain how the ear separates sounds by frequency.** This explanation comes from the work of **Georg von Békésy**, who received the **Nobel Prize in 1961** for discovering how the inner ear responds to sound.
**Inside the inner ear is a long, tapered membrane called the basilar membrane.** It is wide at one end and narrow at the other, and its physical properties change gradually along its length.
children: At the **wide end**, the membrane has **large mass** and **small stiffness**. It is heavy and loose. At the **narrow end**, it has **small mass** and **large stiffness**. It is light and stiff. Moving from the wide end to the narrow end, mass steadily decreases and stiffness steadily increases.

teaching.text: **Applying perturbation theory to each location on the membrane gives each location its own preferred frequency.** At the wide end, large mass lowers the frequency and small stiffness also lowers it, so this end vibrates most strongly for **low-frequency** sounds. At the narrow end, small mass raises the frequency and large stiffness also raises it, so this end vibrates most strongly for **high-frequency** sounds.
children: Every point in between has an intermediate mass and stiffness, so every point is tuned to an intermediate frequency. The membrane is effectively a long row of mass-spring systems, each set to a slightly different frequency.

teaching.text: **Nerve fibers leave the membrane at many locations along its length.** When a particular spot vibrates, the fibers at that spot become active, and which fibers are active tells the brain which frequencies are present in the sound.
children: When a vowel made of two combined frequencies reaches the ear, such as the 1 Hz and 4 Hz combination for /i/, two different places along the membrane vibrate, one for each frequency. The membrane separates the combined vibration back into its component frequencies. This is how the ear can tell /i/ from /a/, since the two vowels are built from different frequency combinations and set different places on the membrane into vibration.

sections.title: Learning rate trades speed for steadiness

teaching.text: **In machine learning, a model is trained by repeatedly updating a value to move it toward a target.** The **learning rate**, written γ, sets how large each update is, as a fraction of the remaining distance to the target. Each full round of updates through the training data is an **epoch**.
**The effect of γ can be seen by training three runs that start near 130, 80 and 10 and all head toward a target of about 80, tracked over 300 epochs at four learning rates.**
children: At a **learning rate of 1 percent**, the runs move smoothly and slowly. The run starting at 130 is still at about 82 after 300 epochs, and the run starting at 10 has only reached about 76. The motion is very steady, but the runs have not fully reached the target.
At a **learning rate of 10 percent**, the runs reach the neighborhood of 80 within roughly the first 30 to 50 epochs and then stay close to it with small wiggles of a few units.

At a **learning rate of 50 percent**, the runs jump to the region of 80 within a few epochs and then bounce noisily, roughly between 70 and 95. At **80 percent**, they arrive almost immediately but bounce even more widely, roughly between 68 and 97, for all 300 epochs.

teaching.text: **These results are the fundamental learning tradeoff.** **When γ increases, speed increases and accuracy decreases.** Large updates get the value to the target region quickly, but the same large updates keep throwing it past the target, so it oscillates around the answer instead of settling. **When γ decreases, speed decreases and accuracy increases.** Small updates keep the value on a smooth, steady path but take many more epochs to arrive.
children: This is the **oscillation in SGD** that appears among the everyday examples of vibration. A high learning rate turns training into a back-and-forth swinging motion around the target.

teaching.text: **The tradeoff is unfortunate, since in practice both fast learning and accurate learning are wanted at the same time.** **Thousands of people, over generations, have made their living by finding better ways to optimize**, meaning better training methods that raise both speed and accuracy together. The goal is a method where **speed increases** and **accuracy increases** at once, escaping the tradeoff that a single fixed learning rate forces.

sections.title: Dynamical Systems 6
Exam reminder
A spring alone and a mass–spring system

teaching.text: **A spring stops at a place, but a mass stops after a process.** This single idea separates two very different kinds of motion. A spring with no mass attached returns to one location and stays there. A spring with a mass attached keeps moving past that location, back and forth, before it finally comes to rest.
children: Everything is measured with one number, the **displacement x**, how far the end of the spring is from its **natural position**, where the spring rests when nothing is pulling or pushing on it. The natural position is x at 0, a stretch to the right is plus 1, and a squeeze to the left is minus 1.

teaching.text: **The spring alone, pulled out to plus 1 and let go, pulls itself back and stops exactly at zero without overshooting.** Plotted against time, the curve starts at plus 1 and bends downward, dropping quickly at first and then more and more slowly. It gets closer and closer to 0 but never crosses below it. The label is **"x approaches 0 without crossing it."**
children: The motion slows because the pull of the spring depends on how far it is stretched. A large stretch produces a large pull back, and a small stretch produces a small pull. As the end gets close to zero, the pull becomes almost zero, so the motion becomes almost zero too.

Pushed in to minus 1 and released, the spring pushes itself back out and settles at zero. The curve starts at minus 1 and rises toward 0, flattening out right at 0 and never going above it. Whether it starts from plus 1 or minus 1, a massless spring always ends at the same place and never passes through it. That is what it means to say a spring **stops at a place**.

teaching.text: **Adding a mass changes the behavior completely.** A mass, drawn as a small cart on wheels, is attached to the free end. Pulled to plus 1 and released, the mass does not stop at zero. It shoots right through the natural position and keeps going to the other side.
children: A moving mass carries its motion with it. When the mass reaches zero, the spring is no longer pulling on it, but the mass is already moving fast, so it continues past zero and compresses the spring on the other side. The compressed spring pushes the mass back, it stops briefly near minus 1, and it is pushed back through zero toward the positive side again. **The mass carries motion through every crossing.**

Plotted against time, x now makes a wave. It starts at plus 1, falls through 0 to nearly minus 1, rises back through 0 to nearly plus 1, and repeats. This repeating back-and-forth motion is called **oscillation**.

teaching.text: **Each swing of the mass is slightly smaller than the one before, so the peaks of the wave shrink a little over time.** This is a **lightly damped oscillation**. **Damping** is anything that slowly drains away the motion, such as friction. With light damping, the mass swings many times before it finally settles at zero.
children: This is why a mass **stops after a process**. It does eventually come to rest at the natural position, but only after a long sequence of crossings, each a little smaller than the last. A mass-spring system therefore has a **frequency**, the number of back-and-forth cycles it completes per second. A massless spring has no frequency at all, because it never swings.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness and the frequencies of speech

teaching.text: **Perturbation theory asks what happens to the behavior of a system when one of its properties is changed.** To **perturb** a system means to nudge one of its settings. For a mass-spring system, the two settings that matter are the **mass m** and the **stiffness k** of the spring, and the behavior of interest is the frequency f of the oscillation.
children: **Increasing the mass decreases the frequency.** A heavier mass is harder to speed up and harder to slow down. The spring pulls with the same strength as before, but that pull changes the heavier mass's speed less. Each swing takes longer, so fewer swings fit into one second. When m goes up, f goes down.

**Increasing the stiffness increases the frequency.** **Stiffness k** is how strongly a spring resists being stretched or squeezed. A stiffer spring pulls back harder for the same stretch, which speeds the mass up faster, so each swing finishes sooner and more swings fit into one second. When k goes up, f goes up.
These two rules are the core of perturbation theory for oscillators. There is no need to calculate an exact frequency to use them. Only the direction the frequency moves matters.

teaching.text: **Speaking changes the effective mass and stiffness of air in the vocal tract.** The **vocal tract** is the air-filled tube from the vocal folds in the throat up through the mouth to the lips. Moving the tongue, jaw and lips squeezes some portions of the air in that tube and opens up others.
children: Squeezing a portion of air changes how much that air acts like a mass and how much it acts like a spring. The **effective mass** and **effective stiffness** of each portion are different for every vowel and every consonant, because each sound uses a different shape of the tube.

The air is set into vibration by the vocal folds. Because the tube has different mass and stiffness in different places, the air vibrates at **many frequencies at once**, and the particular set depends on **where** the air is squeezed and **how much**. So each vowel and consonant has its own set.

teaching.text: **MRI images of five vowels make these shapes visible.** The five words are **dean, dune, done, Dan** and **Don**, which differ only in their vowel. In dean the tongue is high and forward, squeezing the air at the front and leaving it open at the back. In dune the tongue is high but bunched toward the back, with the lips pushed forward. In done the tongue sits in a middle position. In Dan the jaw and tongue are lower and toward the front. In Don the jaw is open widest and the tongue is low and pulled back, squeezing the air in the throat.
children: Each tongue position squeezes the air in a different place and by a different amount, giving a different combination of mass and stiffness and therefore a different set of vibration frequencies. That set is what makes dean sound different from Don.

teaching.text: **The listener has to recover these frequencies from the sound.** The ear has to figure out which low, middle and high frequencies are present in the voice and how strong each one is, and the brain then decides which sound was spoken. Hearing a high frequency of one strength with a low frequency of another might say the word was **"scene,"** while two other frequencies might say **"son."** How the ear separates a single incoming sound into its frequencies is answered by the structure of the inner ear.

sections.title: The cochlea connects incoming sound to neural signals

teaching.text: **Sound is a wave of vibration in the air.** When someone speaks, waves of vibration travel through the air and arrive at the listener's **external ear**, the part on the outside of the head. From there the vibration travels inward through the ear canal toward the **inner ear**.

**The cochlea is the part of the inner ear that reports frequencies to the brain, and it is the one name to know.** It is a small, coiled tube shaped like a snail shell, buried deep inside the bone of the skull. The cochlea sends the brain signals saying which frequencies are present in a sound.

**Enlarged, the inner ear has two main regions.** The upper region holds three looping tubes, the **semicircular ducts**, named anterior, lateral and posterior, with two small sacs, the **utricle** and **saccule**, and small sensory structures called **cristae** inside swellings called **ampullae**. These are part of the inner ear but are not the part that separates sound frequencies.
children: The lower region is the coiled **cochlea**. Three fluid-filled channels run through it side by side, the **vestibular duct**, the **cochlear duct** and the **tympanic duct**, spiraling together around the coil.

The inner ear is a set of soft, membrane-walled tubes, the **membranous labyrinth**, sitting inside matching hollow spaces in hard bone, the **bony labyrinth**. The soft inner tubes are where the sensing happens, and the bone protects them. The **vestibulocochlear nerve** leaves the inner ear and carries the cochlea's signals about frequencies to the brain.

sections.title: The path into the basilar membrane
