The first has one row per recording with **F1 and F2**, and the second has the matching row of **zeros and a single one** that says which vowel it really was. Learning picks a row, computes the network's decision, compares it with the true answer, and changes the weights if the decision is wrong.

**If the network makes the right decision, there is no error, so there is nothing to learn.** This can be a real problem. A network can keep getting the right answer by **memorizing** its data without learning the pattern underneath it, and stopping its learning then would be stopping too early.
Children learning English show the same thing, as **Carol Chomsky** observed in the early 1960s.
children: Very young children first say **go** and **went** correctly, because they are simply **memorizing** what they hear.
Then they notice the real pattern, that most English verbs form the past by adding a sound at the end, as in **jump** and **jumped**, and they start saying **goed**.
Only later do they learn that some verbs are **exceptions**, and they get both the regular verbs and the exceptions right.
In plain terms, getting the right answer early can come from memory, and real learning sometimes shows up as new mistakes.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: The program that trains the network is short, and the exam can ask what its lines mean, though never how to write it from scratch.
children: import torch
from torch import nn
net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 3), nn.Linear(3, 2), nn.Linear(2, 4), nn.Linear(4, 5) )
sgd = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), lr=0.1)
loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(net(X), Y)
loss.backward()
sgd.step()

teaching.text: **The import lines bring into Python the programs for doing inner products, backpropagation and related work**, so none of that has to be written by hand.
children: This works because of **libraries**, collections of programs written by one group that others can use without knowing how they work inside. The idea of software built this way goes back to **Margaret Hamilton's** work on the software that flew **Apollo 11** to the moon.

Around 2015, **Facebook** released **PyTorch** and **Google** released **TensorFlow**, so that researchers no longer had to write their own backpropagation code. Most people now use PyTorch, often just called torch.
The **load** lines read the formant matrix and the matching vowel matrix from files on the computer.

teaching.text: **Sequential means a network that is a sequence of layers**, one after another, which describes every network covered so far. A large language model is an example of a network that is not just a sequence of layers.
children: Each **Linear** line is one **processing layer**, which has weights and does inner products with the information coming in. The input layer does no processing, so the five layers need only **four lines**.
**nn.Linear(2, 3)** says "I receive information from 2 neurons, and I have 3 neurons." The other lines read the same way.

teaching.text: The last lines are all that PyTorch needs for learning.
children: **SGD** is stochastic gradient descent, and **lr** is the **learning rate**, set here to 0.1. **A higher learning rate learns much faster but less accurately, and a lower learning rate learns more accurately but much more slowly.**
So changing the line from a learning rate of 0.1 to 0.3 makes the network **learn faster**, but its **accuracy goes down**.
**Loss** is the **mistake**, and the program calculates the mistakes so it can learn from them.
**backward** is **backpropagation**, and **step** updates the weights.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: Artificial neural networks borrow their basic ideas from discoveries about real brains. There are **neurons**, and each neuron **gathers information from many other neurons**, which is what the inner product does.

**Lord Edgar Adrian**, who won the **Nobel Prize in 1932** for work in the 1920s, discovered that **neurons are nearly digital**. A real neuron is either **firing** or **not firing**, not at some level like 2, 16 or 34. The neurons in the network so far are not like that, since their activations are real numbers like slightly below zero, 6.64, 2.72 and 1.57.
The **sigmoid** is an **activation function** added to the network to work like Adrian's discovery. It takes an inner product and gives back a number between zero and one.
children: An inner product of **minus 4**, minus 6 or minus 1000 gives about **zero**, so the neuron is **off**.
An inner product of **2** gives about 0.8 or 0.9, and **4**, 6 or 100 give about **one**, so the neuron is **on**.
So the sigmoid **digitizes** neural processing, the way brain chemistry does. Without that limit, an activation of a thousand would be like lightning coming out of someone's head.

teaching.text: The sigmoid also reflects perception. **Some things that seem alike are perceived as different, and some things that are very different are perceived as the same.** Very different large negative inputs all come out as off, while two nearly equal inputs on either side of the steep middle come out as off and on.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: Applying the sigmoid one hidden neuron at a time changes the whole calculation downstream. Each neuron's raw inner product is replaced by its sigmoid value, every later activation is recalculated, and the output probabilities shift.
children: The first hidden neuron, slightly below zero, becomes about 0.4, and the second, about 6.6, becomes nearly 1.
With the sigmoid on all nine hidden neurons and the same random weights, the network's choice moves from done to Dan, so it is still wrong until it is trained.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: In the program, **nn.Sigmoid** is added after each hidden linear layer, which means "apply the sigmoid," or make that layer digital. The last layer gets no sigmoid, because its outputs go into the loss calculation.
children: The sigmoid can also be replaced by other functions that look somewhat like it, such as **ReLU**, and trying them out shows whether they improve recognition or make it worse.
**AI is duplicating abilities that animals have.** Its most fundamental ideas come from biologists' discoveries about how brains work, and computer scientists then add ideas of their own on top.

sections.title: One initialization · training the linear network for 2,000 updates

teaching.text: The full training program runs **2000 updates**, each one using all the recordings, with a learning rate of 0.1. The formants are divided by a thousand first, turning hertz into kilohertz, and after every update the program records the **accuracy**, which is the percent of recordings the network classifies correctly. The word with the largest score counts as the network's answer.
**The accuracy starts at 20 percent.** With random weights the network knows nothing, but with **five vowels**, even a random guess is right **one time out of five**. That level is called **chance**.
children: With **ten categories**, chance would be **10 percent**, since a random guess would be right one time in ten.

teaching.text: After a while the accuracy **jumps up to about 40 percent**, so the network is clearly learning something. Then it **levels off**, finishing near **45 percent**. Each pass of learning is called an **epoch**, and it takes thousands of them for a problem like this.

sections.title: Ten initializations · different paths, the same final accuracy

teaching.text: Training was repeated **ten times** on the same data, each time starting from a **different set of random weights**. A starting set of random numbers is called a **seed**, though the word itself will not be asked.
children: The runs take **different paths**. One stays at chance for about 500 epochs before jumping up, another jumps up very early, and another climbs more gradually.
**All ten end at the same accuracy**, close to 45 percent. Learning by stochastic gradient descent always involves chance along the way, but the end point is the same.

teaching.text: Children learning language are similar. One child's home might talk mostly about sports and another's about politics, so each child hears very different words and voices. Yet by about age four, they speak the same language, because the fundamental patterns underneath their different inputs are the same.

**The network levels off near 40 percent, not 100, because the data overlap so much.** For a point in the middle of the overlap, even a person looking carefully at the data would have to squint and guess. AI is not magic, so a problem that is very hard for humans is hard for machines too.
children: Adding or removing layers, or changing the number of neurons in each layer, is the next experiment, to see whether those changes improve on the 40 percent or make it worse.

sections.title: NNs → LLMs → Agentic Systems
Neural networks, 1943–1986 · a static vector and a few categories

teaching.text: A **neural network** takes in information about one moment, uses its **weights** to process it and makes a decision, and it learns those weights by making errors and correcting them through **backpropagation**. The idea began in **1943** with a paper by **McCulloch and Pitts**, which proposed that simple mathematics could model how the brain works.
children: The paper starts from the **all-or-none** character of nervous activity, where all means active and none means inactive. That is the same idea as the **sigmoid**, so the very first paper on artificial neural networks starts from biology about how real neurons behave.
Warren McCulloch was a **psychiatrist**, and the earliest work on neural networks aimed to model how the mind works, including mental illness, not to make money.

teaching.text: By **1986**, the ideas had matured into the two **Parallel Distributed Processing** books, written by a group at UC San Diego. **Parallel** means many neurons compute their activations at the same time, and **distributed** means the information from the inputs is spread across all the neurons. Forward propagation and backpropagation were well formed by then, and one contributor, **Geoffrey Hinton**, later won the **2024 Nobel Prize in Physics** for this work.

**Given some static vector of formants, these networks could make a decision about a few possible categories.** A **vector** is just a list of numbers, and static means one fixed list from one moment. But **human cognition is far more complex** than taking in one list of numbers and giving one decision at the end.
children: **Speech is incredibly time-varying**, because every little moment in time gives a new set of formants.
**Language is time-varying too**, since a sentence is a whole bunch of words, one after another.
So giving a network one bunch of numbers can never model cognition that unfolds in time.

sections.title: Jordan’s recurrent network for speech production

teaching.text: In **1985**, **Michael Jordan** developed **recurrent neural networks** to make sense of **speech production**, meaning how the tongue, the velum and the lips move over time. Features such as nasality, backness and lip rounding each switch on and off at different moments across a sequence of sounds, and he realized that a regular network could never handle something that complex and time-varying.
children: His network is **not just sequential**, one layer after another, because it has **two layers working in parallel**.

It is called **recurrent** because it **takes its output and sends it back into part of its input**. It produces something at one moment, then uses that to predict the next moment, and then the moment after that.

teaching.text: **GPT works the same way, one word at a time.** It takes the words of the prompt and predicts the next word, which becomes the first word of its answer. Then it feeds the prompt plus that word back in and predicts the next word again, and keeps going. So the idea behind GPT starts in 1985 with thinking about how speech unfolds in time.
children: People kept refining the recurrent network from 1985 until **2017**, when the **large language model** was invented.

teaching.text: **Science and technology evolve from other people's ideas over long stretches of time.** An idea from 1943 was refined into the networks of 1986, and Jordan's idea from 1985 was refined into the large language models of 2017. The people who came up with these ideas were mostly not the ones who made a lot of money from them.
children: These years give a sense of the history, but they will not be asked about.

sections.title: From one neuron to agentic systems

teaching.text: AI systems build up in steps, and **each step is made of the one before it**.
children: **A single neuron takes in a vector and gives back one number.** It multiplies each input by its weight and adds them all up, which is the **inner product**, and the symbol **sigma** just means add them up. This uses nothing but second-grade multiplication and addition to model the electrochemical activity of a real neuron.
**A neural network takes in one vector and gives back a whole decision vector.** Its layers are linked by sets of weights, and each set turns one vector into the next through many inner products.

teaching.text: **A large language model takes in many vectors, one for each moment in a sequence, and gives back one decision vector about what comes next.** Picture 15 vectors, each standing for something at one moment, such as one word of a sentence. The job of the model is to **predict the sixteenth**.
children: In real systems, the vectors number in the hundreds of thousands to a million, and that set is called the **context window**. Each vector is also thousands of numbers long, which is why huge data centers are needed.
The sixteenth vector is a **probability distribution over the next word**. With about 30,000 English words, each entry gives the likelihood that one particular word comes next.

teaching.text: **A large language model is made of neural networks.** Each set of weights is a **layer**, and real systems have about a hundred or more layers. **The knowledge is still in the weights**, so an LLM's knowledge of how to write an essay is stored in its weights.

**An LLM is a dynamical system**, and that is why the Nobel Prize for AI was awarded in physics. A mass-spring system starts from **initial conditions** and the system decides what happens next. An LLM's initial condition is its set of input vectors, and each layer turns them into **better vectors**, step after step, until the last layer can predict the next word.
children: The calculation at every step is the **inner product**, multiplying and adding billions or trillions of times.
In plain terms, an LLM is like the oscillator, except that instead of two numbers changing over time, thousands of numbers are refined layer by layer.

teaching.text: **An LLM learns by predicting the next word and correcting its mistakes.** Given "the cat sat on the," with **mat** as the real next word, a new LLM with random weights might predict something impossible like "in." Backpropagation adjusts its trillions of weights so the prediction moves toward mat.
children: Repeating this with about a trillion sentences, the system surprisingly ends up knowing how to speak English. No philosopher or cognitive scientist would have expected that human language could be emulated with inner products and functions like the sigmoid.
The first problem this design solved, in 2017, was **machine translation**, and the same design then worked for speech and many other problems.

teaching.text: **An agentic system is a graph of LLMs**, and an **agent** in AI today is just an LLM.
children: An **outline LLM** receives the prompt and is instructed only to outline the answer.
A **writing LLM** turns the outline into smooth sentences.
A **critic LLM** criticizes the draft, and a **revision LLM** decides whether it is good enough or sends it back to the critic. The back-and-forth is usually limited to a few rounds.
A **final LLM** produces the output the user sees.
The critic is what greatly reduced **hallucination**, the system making things up, and the inner conversation between LLMs is why many systems take a while to respond.

teaching.text: The layers of this build-up mirror living things. **Neurons make neural networks, neural networks make LLMs, and LLMs make agentic systems**, much as molecules make cells and cells make organs.
children: Designing a graph of LLMs to solve a problem is a real job today, and it needs problem solving more than knowledge of programming languages.

The connections between LLMs can also form circuits nobody planned, which let a system call on other LLMs and do things that were never part of the design, sometimes harmful ones. Limiting those connections is a problem that needs creative people from many fields.

teaching.text: **The chief insight behind all of this is Gestalt completion.** People see a triangle in the Gestalt figure even though none is drawn, because a big part of human knowledge is **completing** what is missing. Training a system only to **predict the missing thing** turns out to emulate human cognition.
children: The same idea is behind the **cloze procedure**, a test introduced by **Wilson Taylor** in **1953**, in which words are deleted from a text and people fill them in. The name comes from **closure**, the Gestalt term for completing a familiar pattern that is not quite finished, such as seeing a broken circle as whole.
**Knowledge can be tested by asking someone to complete a sequence, and for AI, completion is all that knowledge is.** An LLM predicting the next word is playing a cloze game over and over.
Underneath everything, **inference is inner products**, and **learning is stochastic gradient descent plus dynamic programming**.

sections.title: Fifteen vectors · the same next-item question for any sequence

teaching.text: **An LLM takes 15 vectors and predicts the sixteenth**, and since a vector is just a list of numbers, those numbers can stand for almost anything. Whatever they stand for, the machine plays the same game of predicting the next one.

The vectors can be **words**. In "The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the," the sixteenth vector is the missing next word, and a speaker of English knows a likely completion, such as branch or mat.
children: Getting it right means using the whole sentence, since it was the cat, not the dog, that sat.

teaching.text: The vectors can be **slices of sound**. A spectrogram is cut into little frames, each frame becomes one vector of frequencies and amplitudes, and the system learns to predict the next little piece of speech from all the previous pieces.
children: This approach, in 2019, gave the **best speech recognition in 75 years**, and it is also the basis for synthetic voices that are now very hard to tell from humans.
The newest systems can hold a spoken conversation, and the only giveaway left is a slight delay before each response. As that delay shrinks, phone scams become a real danger.

teaching.text: The vectors can be **pieces of an image**. An image is cut into **16 patches** read row by row, and the system predicts the missing patch. Trained on huge numbers of images, it learns what a dog, a dolphin or a boat is, and this became the basis of modern **computer vision**.

The vectors can even be **amino acids**. A protein is a string of amino acids, which come in **20 kinds**, and the order of the string decides how the protein folds into its shape. Treating a protein as just a sequence and playing the same predict-the-next game pushed the **protein folding problem** many years ahead, which matters for designing drugs and vaccines.
children: That work won the **2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry**.

teaching.text: **The LLM only ever sees vectors.** Words, sounds, pixels and molecules all reach it the same way, so one design asks one question, what comes sixteenth, every time.
children: Because these systems predict from past data, something new that the past data does not cover can make them **hallucinate**. A forecast far into an unfamiliar future can end up as a guess, or as an honest "I don't know."

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: English allows only **certain sequences of sounds** in its words, and knowing which sequences are allowed is part of every speaker's knowledge of the language. **A simple English syllable can have a consonant, then a vowel, then a consonant**, as in Don, mat, sit, cup, dog and fish.
children: The pattern is about **sounds, not letters**. The silent e in shave, kite and rope does not count, and two letters can spell one consonant sound, as in ship, chin and bath.

teaching.text: Syllables can also have **clusters**, which are groups of consonants together. A cluster before the vowel is an **onset**, as in split, flat and black, and a cluster after the vowel is a **coda**, as in desk, help and lamp. **Only certain sequences are allowed before the vowel and after the vowel.**
children: Each real word has an impossible twin marked with a star, such as **flat** and **lfat**, **help** and **hepl**, and **lamp** and **lapm**. Many twins use the same letters in the other order, so order matters.

**The order mirrors around the vowel.** In flat, the l sits right next to the vowel with the f farther out. In help, the l again sits next to the vowel, now on the other side, with the p farther out. Each impossible twin puts the wrong consonant against the vowel.
A made-up product name like "desb" or "lapm" sounds instantly un-English, because it breaks these rules.

teaching.text: **A long word is a chain of syllables**, such as ba-na-na, At-lan-tic and ath-lete. The sounds t and l are fine across a syllable break, but **tl cannot start a syllable**, which is why Atlantic is a word but tlantic is impossible.
children: The sound **ng** can end a syllable, as in ring, but it can never start one.
So whether a sequence of sounds is allowed depends on where the syllable breaks fall.

teaching.text: **Every language has its own rules.** Mandarin allows only nasal sounds at the end of a syllable, Cantonese also allows a final p, as in cup, and Russian and Polish allow clusters like zb or dl at the start of a word, which English never does. Spanish speakers turn a word like stadium into one that starts with e, so that each syllable avoids an s-t onset.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: **Phonotactic knowledge can be revealed by the same next-item game that GPT plays.** Each item is the start of an English word, and the task is to guess the next letter. People agree on their guesses quickly, and how much they agree changes from item to item.
**After a vowel, almost anything can follow.** After "ra," likely letters include t, n, r and l, and many others are possible too.
**At the start of a word, the choices narrow sharply** to exactly what an English onset allows.
children: After **sp**, the next letter is l, r or a vowel, and never n.
After **k**, it is a vowel or n, as in knee, and never t.
After **b** and **f**, it is r, l or a vowel, and never n.
After **sh**, it is a vowel or r, as in shrimp.
After **skr** or **m** at the start of a word, only a vowel can come.
After **bram**, the letter b is almost forced, as in bramble, though a new syllable could also start there.

teaching.text: **Guessing the next letter is predicting the sixteenth item**, the same next-token game an LLM plays. A GPT trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling, because its predictions can only get good by matching the patterns of English syllables.
children: Its prediction is a **probability distribution** over the next letter, and the shape of that distribution carries the knowledge.
After "ra," the distribution is **flat**, spread over many letters, while after "skr" it is **sharply peaked** on a few vowels, because English allows nothing else there.
In plain terms, the more the letters so far restrict what can come next, the more the probability piles onto a few letters.

sections.title: Build an LLM together

teaching.text: English syllables are a good test case for understanding LLMs. English has about 30,000 words, so training on words needs enormous data, but it has only about 26 letters, or a few dozen sounds. So a small LLM, with thousands of weights instead of trillions, can be trained to learn the knowledge of English syllables that every speaker already has.

Instead of writing that program by hand, which would take months, the plan is to **design an agentic system using instructions written in English**. The agentic system builds the LLM, trains it to predict each next letter, and shows what it has learned along the way, so it can be compared with the knowledge of English syllables that speakers carry in their heads.

lecture18.title: Neuron, Neural Networks, LLMs and Agents

sections.title: Neuron, neural networks, LLMs and agents
From a neuron to agents that communicate

teaching.text: Everything in modern AI grows from **one very simple idea**. A **neuron** takes information from other neurons, multiplies each input by its weight and adds them up, which is the **inner product**. That arithmetic stands in for neurons communicating electrochemically. People who move science forward usually start from extremely simple ideas like this one and then multiply them many times over.
children: A **neural network** repeats that operation layer after layer, taking a vector in and giving a **decision** out. Even something as complex as a person making a decision can be built from inner products and a function like the sigmoid, combined many times.
But a network that makes one **static decision**, such as hearing one vowel from two formants, cannot capture cognition that **unfolds in time**.

teaching.text: **Language depends on long-distance relationships between words.** In "the dog that my parents, who I love very much, who live in a state far, far away," the next word is **barks**, not bark.
children: **Barks** goes with the singular **dog**, no matter how many other words come in between, even plural ones like parents.

No one teaches this rule explicitly. Speakers absorb it from the language around them, and an LLM learns it the same way, from data, by using its weights to do inner products, then more inner products, until it predicts barks.
English sentence structure, or **syntax**, is so complicated that many linguists spend their careers on it, and that is why an LLM needs so many layers of computation.

teaching.text: **LLMs can be multilingual and multimodal.** The first use of LLMs, in 2017, was **translation** between languages, which is now nearly solved for hundreds of languages.
children: A system trained on several languages, such as English, Dutch and Japanese, learns how words go together in general, so it also gets good at very different languages, such as Navajo.
**Multimodal** systems connect different modes, such as text, speech and images, so they can caption a photo or create an image from a spoken description.

teaching.text: **Nobody fully understands what all the weights are doing.** The designs were not planned from scratch. Over about 75 years, people tinkered with something that worked a little, changed it so it worked a little better, and kept going, much as dogs were bred over a few hundred years into today's breeds. Researchers around the world are now trying to figure out what the weights do, partly so that much smaller, less wasteful systems could be built.

**An agentic system is a team of LLMs that talk to each other in English.** An outline LLM plans the answer, a writing LLM writes it, a critic LLM checks whether each statement follows from the one before, and a revision LLM loops with the critic, sometimes under a **controller** agent that passes work between them.
children: The agents are also **multilingual in computer languages**, such as Python and database languages, because they were trained to predict whole programs too.

Once each LLM is trained, its weights are usually **not trained further** while the agents work together. Some new systems are starting to learn their own connections, which makes them partly self-designing.

Agents share a **common memory** where they can write and read information. That shared memory is a big source of their power and also of the danger, because it lets them coordinate in ways nobody planned.

The same tools can do good work. One agentic system acts as a patient teacher for a nearly lost Native American language, even though there is far too little text in that language to train an ordinary LLM on it.

sections.title: Parallel heads and successive layers

teaching.text: **Predicting the next word is so difficult that an LLM needs many layers, and in each layer it needs many parallel heads.** A head is a separate expert, and in each layer the knowledge from all the heads is brought together to produce **improved vectors**. Then the same thing happens again in the next layer.
children: This is a question for the exam, so the structure matters. **Layers go one after another from the input to the output, and heads sit side by side within each layer.**

teaching.text: **A classroom comparison makes heads and layers clear.** Imagine trying to improve oneself by visiting a series of classes, one after another.
children: In the first class, each student is asked for an independent opinion on how to improve. Each student is like a **head**, an expert with its own view.
All of those opinions are then **combined** to make one improved version. That combining is what a layer does with the opinions of its heads.
Then the next class is visited, and the same thing happens again. **The classes are the layers.**
In plain terms, layers give an LLM its depth, one round of improvement after another, and heads give it width, many experts consulted at once within each round.

teaching.text: **Each head is a set of weights**, and an expert's knowledge is in its weights. Every head in every layer learns how to improve the vectors so that, at the very end, the next word can be predicted.
children: Large systems have **a hundred or more layers** and on the order of **a hundred heads** in each layer, which shows how complicated language, vision and the other things these systems handle really are.

The heads and layers are trained the same way as everything else. A sentence like "the dog that ... barks" is taken from text, the system predicts the next word, and if it predicts the wrong word, **every head in every layer** adjusts its weights through backpropagation so the next prediction is closer to barks.
Doing this at scale uses enormous resources. In some states, a large share of the water goes to the data centers that run this training.

sections.title: A dynamical rule across time and depth

teaching.text: **A dynamical system is a rule that is fed back to itself.** Numbers go in, the rule acts on them, numbers come out, and the output is fed back in as the next input, again and again. The overall goal is to understand the general structure, not to memorize formulas.
children: In the **harmonic oscillator**, the two numbers are the position x and the velocity v. Starting with x at one and v at zero, the first step leaves x the same and makes v go down.
x and v **take turns**. The new x is computed from the old v, and then the new v is computed from that new x. Step by step, the rule draws a **cosine** for x.
Fields as far apart as finance use the same idea with different rules. Stock prices are modeled with equations that are fed back on themselves, though the real market never follows them exactly.

teaching.text: **Jordan's network was a marriage of neural networks and dynamical systems.** Based on the time variation in speech production, Jordan designed a network whose **output is copied back into its state units**, which also keep a fading copy of their own previous values.
children: **Plan units** and **state units** feed the hidden layer, the hidden layer feeds the output, and the output loops back into the state. The same weights are used at every step.
After more than **thirty years of tinkering**, this idea became the **LLM**.

teaching.text: **In an LLM, the layer is the rule.** Each layer applies its weights to every vector, and the next layer works on the result, so **depth plays the role of time**. Following one number up through the layers traces out a curve, much like the oscillator's curve, though not an exact cosine.
children: So the LLM is an unrolled recurrent network, laid out layer by layer, just as the spring's motion was laid out step by step when it was computed on a computer.
The rule in each layer is the weights of its heads, and those weights are learned through backpropagation by predicting the next word.
Agentic systems also contain loops, such as the critic and revision loop, so dynamical systems run all the way up through AI.
The mathematics of inner products that LLMs depend on was first studied deeply in **quantum mechanics**, about a hundred years ago, so physics and AI are closely tied in more ways than one.

sections.title: One prediction task for different sequences

teaching.text: An LLM is given **15 vectors** and asked to predict the **16th**, and the vectors can come from anywhere, because the machine only ever sees lists of numbers.
children: They can be **15 words** of a sentence, such as "The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the," with the next word missing.
They can be **15 frames of a spectrogram**, with the next slice of speech missing.
They can be **15 patches of an image**, read row by row, with the bottom-right patch missing.
They can be **15 amino acids** in a protein. In the B chain of insulin, the residue that follows the first fifteen is the amino acid written Y.

teaching.text: **The same design and the same prediction game work for language, speech, vision and proteins.** Whatever the vectors stand for, the job is always to predict what comes next in the sequence.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: English has about 30,000 words, so training an LLM on words takes enormous data, money and energy. But speakers also know a much smaller system made of **only a few dozen sounds**, which is how vowels and consonants can follow each other to make words. Because there are so few sounds, an LLM for this system can be small enough to study closely.
**A simple English syllable is a consonant, then a vowel, then a consonant**, as in Don, sit, shave, cup, dog and fish. The pattern is about sounds, so the silent e of shave does not count.
children: English also allows **clusters**, as in split, flat, black, glad, desk, help and milk. Only certain clusters are allowed, so **sblit**, **lfat**, **desb** and **lapm** are impossible, and a product called "desb" would sound instantly un-English.
Long words are chains of syllables. **Atlantic** is fine because t and l sit across a syllable break, but **tlantic** is impossible, because tl cannot start an English syllable.

teaching.text: **Every language has its own rules for sequences**, and speakers absorb them without being taught.
children: **Mandarin** allows only nasal sounds at the end of a syllable, so words like mat, sit and shave are impossible in it.
**Cantonese** also allows a final p, as in cup.
**Russian and Polish** allow clusters like zb or dl at the start of a word, which English never allows.
**Spanish** does not allow an s and t to start a word, so speakers add an e at the start of a word like stadium, keeping each syllable simple.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: Guessing the next letter of an English word reveals this sound knowledge directly. **After a vowel, almost anything can follow**, but **at the start of a word the choices narrow sharply**.
children: After **sp**, only l, r or a vowel can come, and after **skr** or a word-initial **m**, only a vowel can come.
After **k**, a vowel or n can come, as in knee, and after **sh**, a vowel or r, as in shrimp.

teaching.text: **Guessing the next letter is predicting the 16th vector.** A GPT that only plays this game learns English sounds and spelling. Its predicted probability distribution is **flat** after a vowel and **sharply peaked** after skr, because English allows almost nothing else there.

sections.title: Design an agentic system for English syllables

teaching.text: An LLM that learns English syllables can be built by **describing it in English** to an agentic system, instead of programming it by hand. The request specified **five layers**, **four heads in each layer**, and **input vectors 64 numbers long**.
children: It asked the system to pick **1000 English words at random** and train the LLM on them, taking each letter and trying to **predict the next letter**, then improving the weights to predict better.
It also asked the system to show **ten generated words after each step of training**, to reveal what the LLM currently knew about English.

teaching.text: The agentic system understood the request in its own technical terms. It built a small **character-level transformer**, another name for an LLM that works letter by letter, with **attention heads**.
children: **Attention** means a head consults the rest of the sequence to work out which preceding items matter, just as predicting barks requires attending to dog.
It chose to train on **pronunciations** instead of spellings, so the silent e in shave would not mislead it, and it wrote the program in Python on its own.

teaching.text: The results show how hard the problem is. After training on 1000 words, the generated words were **still mostly gibberish**, with perhaps a few vowels starting to appear in the right places. Training on **10,000 words** and for many more steps was the suggested next change. A choice that seems easy for any speaker, such as which sounds can follow which, is not easy even for an LLM.
This way of working has a name.
children: **Software 1.0** is writing programs in a programming language such as Python or C.
**Software 2.0** is giving a neural network input data and output data, so the program becomes the **weights** that predict the outputs from the inputs.

**Software 3.0** is using an agentic system, a set of LLMs talking to each other and to the user, to build and run a program. Doing this with plain English instructions is called **vibe coding**, and it means someone with a good idea no longer needs to hire a programmer to build it.

teaching.text: The first attempt at this kind of problem was in **Claude Shannon's 1948 paper, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication."** Working by hand, Shannon generated sequences of letters that came closer and closer to English, from random strings of consonants to strings with vowels and real short words.
children: That paper founded **information theory**, one of the most important fields in engineering, and it remains important for LLMs today.
**Viterbi**, one of the developers of dynamic programming, published his most famous work in an information theory journal, so the ideas behind backpropagation and LLMs share the same roots.
